rv.q: 'Love' is a great piece of theater — funny, beautifully staged, and with the kind of excitement that retunes your attention to tiny heartbreaks instead of just huge ones
The small, close-up gestures, piece by piece, add up to a captivating whole.
Even with minimal dialogue, the performances from all the actors are so finely etched that a certain sad warmth and sense of camaraderie with them accrues.
The portrait is veristic, timely, and compellingly dramatic.
It's an astonishing piece, and, in its quiet, unmelodramatic way, it demands to be seen.
For those open to a different kind of theater (and sitting up front), the love really does come through.
The emotional stir of Zeldin’s play exists in this lacuna.
However, LOVE is a valuable record of life in a shelter using a documentary approach that is so real that it makes us feel like voyeurs.
The play could have easily become deadly tiresome if not for the brilliant cast.
Otherwise, LOVE is easy to admire but not that easy to love.
The extraordinary performances, understated and never actorly, reinforce the vérité quality of Zeldin’s script.
That this is gripping theater and occasionally harrowing is a testament to the uniformly excellent performances.

cn.t: Zeldin's immersive drama about homelessness earns praise for its naturalistic staging and empathetic performances, though critics split on whether its understated, slice-of-life approach is powerfully urgent or dramatically inert.
